name: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra and Friends
intent: Know why Dijkstra's greedy choice works and exactly when it stops working (negative weights), what the heap buys you and when it does not, what Bellman-Ford costs for being safe, and how A* uses a heuristic to search less and when that heuristic silently costs you the shortest path.
scenario: A routing service finds the cheapest path between two points on a weighted graph. Dijkstra with a heap is fast on the road-like test graph (9,557 steps for 1,000 nodes against 602,800 for the array version). Then costs gain refunds and discounts, so some edges become negative, and the same code keeps answering, quickly and confidently, with distances that are too long for 992 of 1,000 nodes. An A* variant tuned for speed returns a path of cost 210 where 198 was possible.
problem: Shortest-path algorithms look interchangeable until their assumptions break. Dijkstra needs every edge weight to be non-negative and fails silently without it. A heap is the textbook companion, but whether it beats a plain array depends on how dense the graph is and how often relaxations succeed. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges and detects negative cycles, at a higher worst-case price. A* can search a small fraction of the graph, but only gives the shortest path if its estimate never promises more than is possible.

howItWorks.title: Dijkstra: settle the closest node, then relax its edges
howItWorks.text: Keep a distance estimate for every node, starting at infinity except the source at 0. Repeatedly pick the unsettled node with the smallest estimate, call it settled, and relax each of its edges: if going through this node gives a neighbour a smaller estimate, update it. Why a settled distance is final: every other route to that node must pass through some unsettled node whose estimate is at least as large, and with non-negative weights a path only gets longer as it goes on. Everything depends on that sentence, and the next steps show what happens when it is false.

howItWorks.title: Array or heap: the answer depends on the graph
howItWorks.text: Finding the closest unsettled node is the only choice to make. With a plain array you scan all V nodes each time: V steps per node, about V squared in all, plus the edge checks. With a binary heap you push an entry whenever a distance improves and pop the smallest, so the cost is the edge checks plus about log V steps for each push and pop. On a sparse graph of 1,000 nodes and 3,000 edges that is 9,557 steps against 602,800. On a dense graph of 1,000 nodes and 499,500 edges where most relaxations improve nothing, the heap still wins (266,979 against 752,000). The heap loses when almost every edge improves a distance, so each one pays a push: 18,148,855 steps against 1,500,500 for the array. The textbook bounds, E log V for the heap and V squared for the array, are worst cases, and the real count depends on how many relaxations succeed. Most library heaps have no decrease-key, so the usual code pushes a duplicate and skips stale entries when they surface.

howItWorks.title: Negative weights break Dijkstra, silently
howItWorks.text: If an edge can be negative, a path can get shorter as it goes on, so a settled node may still be improved later. Take A to B costing 3, A to C costing 5, C to B costing -4, and B to D costing 1. The textbook Dijkstra used here settles each node once and never expands it again, so it settles B at 3, passes that on to D (4), and only then finds that going through C gets B down to 1. The code does not crash and the loop finishes: D is left at 4 where the true answer is 2. On a layered graph of 1,000 nodes with weights from -4 to 10, the result was wrong for 992 of 1,000 nodes, too long by up to 199. Negative weights are real (refunds, discounts, rebates in a cost graph, and exchange rates turned into costs with logarithms), and adding a constant to every edge does not repair them, because paths with more edges then pay the constant more times and the ranking of paths changes. A variant that expands a node again whenever its distance drops (a lazy heap version that skips an entry only if it is larger than the current distance, rather than when the node is already settled) gets this small example right and is correct whenever no negative cycle exists, but it loses Dijkstra's time bound and can take exponential time in the worst case.

howItWorks.title: Bellman-Ford: relax everything until nothing improves
howItWorks.text: Bellman-Ford sweeps all edges, relaxing each, and repeats. A shortest path has at most V - 1 edges, so after V - 1 sweeps every distance is final, and it stops early when a sweep changes nothing: 5,988 edge checks in 2 rounds on the 1,000-node negative graph. It is correct with negative edges, and one more sweep that still improves something proves a negative cycle is reachable (3 rounds on the smallest example): then no shortest path exists, because every lap lowers the cost. The price is the worst case of V times E: on a chain whose edges point against the order the nodes are swept, 1,000 nodes need 500,499 edge checks in 1,000 rounds where Dijkstra needs 999. An undirected graph with one negative edge has a negative cycle, because the edge can be walked back and forth.

howItWorks.title: A*: Dijkstra with an estimate of what is left
howItWorks.text: A* picks the node with the smallest cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to the goal, so it heads toward the goal instead of spreading in every direction. If the estimate never exceeds the true remaining cost (admissible), the first time the goal is settled its path is a shortest path, provided closed nodes may be reopened; a version that never reopens them, like the one in the samples, also needs the estimate to be consistent (it drops by at most the edge cost along any edge). The Manhattan distance on a grid with unit moves is both. On a 100 by 100 grid with a few blocked cells, the Manhattan distance expands 652 nodes against 9,092 for Dijkstra (an estimate of 0 is exactly Dijkstra), and both find a path of cost 198. The heuristic is a promise. Tripling it expands only 211 nodes but returns cost 210: it believed the goal was farther than it was, so it committed to a worse route. Some systems choose that trade deliberately for speed; it should be a decision, not an accident.

pros: Dijkstra settles each node once, so with a heap it costs about (V + E) log V, far below V squared on sparse graphs
Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and tells you when a negative cycle makes the question meaningless
A* searches toward the goal and can expand a small fraction of the nodes Dijkstra does
All three fit one idea, relaxation, so one implementation can be adapted to the others
cons: Dijkstra gives wrong distances without any error as soon as one edge is negative
A binary heap can cost more than a plain array on dense graphs where every edge improves a distance
Bellman-Ford costs up to V times E, much slower than Dijkstra on large graphs
A* is only as good as its heuristic: a weak one is slow, an overestimating one is not optimal, an expensive one eats the gain
whenToUse: Dijkstra: cheapest routes with non-negative costs from one source to many targets, such as link-state routing (OSPF runs a shortest-path-first computation) or delivery costs
Bellman-Ford: graphs with negative weights, negative-cycle detection (such as an arbitrage check), and the distance-vector idea behind protocols like RIP
A*: one source to one goal where a good distance estimate exists, such as grids, maps and game worlds
BFS instead of any of these, when all edges cost the same
whenNotToUse: Dijkstra on a graph that can contain negative edges: use Bellman-Ford, or reweight the graph first with a method such as Johnson's
A heap on a small dense graph without measuring: a plain array scan can be cheaper and simpler
A* with a heuristic you have not shown to be admissible, if the shortest path is required
Bellman-Ford on a huge graph with only non-negative weights, where Dijkstra does the same job in far fewer steps
pitfalls: Running the settle-once Dijkstra on negative weights: it finishes with no error and was wrong for 992 of 1,000 nodes, too long by up to 199; check the weights when the graph is built, or fail loudly
Fixing negative weights by adding a constant to every edge: a path with more edges pays the constant more times, so the shortest path itself can change

Using INT_MAX as infinity and then adding an edge weight to it: in a fixed-width integer that wraps to a huge negative number and looks like the best distance of all; use a sentinel and check it, or a value with headroom
Assuming a heap is always faster than an array: on a dense graph where every relaxation improves a distance it needed 18,148,855 steps against 1,500,500, so measure on your own graph shape

Forgetting to skip stale heap entries: with duplicate pushes instead of decrease-key the heap took 499,501 pushes for 1,000 nodes on the dense graph where every relaxation improves a distance, and a stale entry that is processed again repeats edge checks or corrupts results
Reporting Bellman-Ford distances when a negative cycle is reachable: the numbers keep dropping with every round, and the only correct answer is that no shortest path exists
Treating a negative undirected edge as a one-way cost: an undirected negative edge can be walked back and forth, which is a negative cycle
Using a heuristic that overestimates and expecting the shortest path: 3 times the Manhattan distance returned a path of cost 210 where 198 was possible, with no sign that anything was off
Using Dijkstra or A* when BFS would do: if all edges cost the same, a plain queue finds the fewest-edges path without a heap

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: Asks for the cheapest route from a source, to one goal or to every node.

roles.label: Weighted graph
roles.description: Nodes, and edges with a cost that may or may not be negative.

roles.label: Priority queue
roles.description: A heap or an array that hands out the closest unsettled node.

roles.label: Distance table
roles.description: The best known cost to each node, lowered by relaxation.

roles.label: Heuristic
roles.description: A guess of the cost still to go, used by A* to steer the search.

quiz.question: A weighted graph with no cycles has one edge with weight -4. What can happen when you run the textbook Dijkstra, which settles each node once and never expands it again?
options: It stops with an error at the first negative weight it meets.
It finishes normally, but some distances can be too long.
It returns correct distances, just with more steps than usual.
It loops forever on any graph that has a negative edge.
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra settles a node when it is the closest unsettled one, trusting that no later path can be shorter. A negative edge breaks that trust, but the code has no check for it, so it finishes and returns distances that can be too long, with no error. Only a variant that re-expands nodes whose distance drops would be correct here, and it can need far more steps.

quiz.question: A graph of 1,000 nodes has about 500,000 edges, and almost every relaxation lowers a distance. Which Dijkstra implementation does less work?
options: The heap, since a heap is never slower than scanning for the minimum.
Both cost about the same, since the edge checks dominate either way.
The array: a flat V steps per node beats a heap climb for every edge.
Neither can run, since a graph with this many edges has no shortest path.
quiz.explanation: Every improving relaxation pushes a new heap entry that must climb, so the heap needed 18,148,855 steps here against 1,500,500 for the array. On sparse graphs, or when most relaxations improve nothing, the heap wins by a wide margin.

quiz.question: An A* search uses a heuristic that sometimes overestimates the distance left to the goal. What can you expect?
options: It stays optimal but expands more nodes than Dijkstra would.
It behaves exactly like Dijkstra, because the estimate is ignored.
It stops with an error when the estimate is larger than the real cost.
It may expand far fewer nodes, but the path it returns can be longer than the shortest.
quiz.explanation: An overestimate pushes the search toward the goal too eagerly, so it can settle the goal by a worse route before a better one is tried. Tripling the Manhattan distance gave cost 210 after 211 expansions, against 198 for the true shortest path.
